common_name: Little Linda Mountain Laurel (Miniature Fine-Leaf Selection)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil; avoid soggy sites and heavy afternoon sun. Little Linda is a true miniature mountain laurel with foliage scaled to about half the size of the species, ideal for small beds and rock gardens.

directions: Site in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled shade to partial shade, mulching with pine bark or pine straw to hold moisture and acidity. Little Linda, a Richard Jaynes introduction named for his daughter, bears dark red buds that open to near-white flowers and gradually age to a rich pink, held on a tight, regular, slow-growing mound with proportionally miniature leaves — the smallest-leaved mountain laurel cultivar widely grown. Its very compact, tidy habit needs almost no pruning and suits foundation plantings, rock gardens, or the front of a shaded shrub border. Like all mountain laurel, every part of the plant is toxic if ingested.

common_name: Nathan Hale Mountain Laurel (Red Bud, Pink Flower Compact Selection)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil; tolerates more sun than many cultivars but still benefits from afternoon shade in hot climates. Nathan Hale forms a dense, symmetrical, rounded shrub with deep red buds opening to pink flowers.

directions: Plant in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in a site receiving morning sun with afternoon shade to full partial shade. Nathan Hale, selected and named by the Nathan Hale Society of the Sons of the American Revolution to honor Connecticut's Revolutionary War hero, bears deep red buds opening to pink flowers above thick, glossy, dark green foliage, with purplish-red new stems and petioles adding color even before bloom. Its dense, full, symmetrically rounded habit holds its shape with little pruning, making it a strong specimen or foundation shrub. Like all mountain laurel, every part of the plant is toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade to partial shade; Underway is an unusually robust, vigorous Mahonia x media selection from the Slieve Donard Nursery breeding program.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade to deep partial shade, tolerating heavier shade than most flowering evergreen shrubs. Underway, a hybrid of Mahonia japonica and M. lomariifolia raised at the historic Slieve Donard Nursery in Northern Ireland, is one of the largest and most vigorous of the x media selections, bearing bright yellow, fragrant flower spikes in late autumn — earlier than most other mahonias — above bold, holly-like evergreen foliage, followed by powdery blue-black berries. Its outsized eventual scale makes it best suited to a spacious shaded border or woodland-edge planting rather than a tight foundation bed. Water during establishment and dry spells, and prune only to remove dead or leggy canes.

common_name: Chinese Mahonia (Late-Blooming Purplish-Red Flowered Oregon Grape Relative)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; give it a sheltered woodland site since it is less cold-hardy than many mahonias.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath open woodland canopy; Chinese mahonia is a small, open-branching, suckering evergreen shrub native to forest margins and lower alpine slopes of Sichuan and Yunnan. Unlike most mahonias, which flower in winter or spring, it produces loose, pendant racemes of tiny, non-fragrant purplish-red flowers with contrasting yellow centers from late summer into fall, followed by blue-black berries. Its arching, suckering habit and unusual late bloom time make it a distinctive addition to a shaded woodland border where its off-season color extends garden interest. Prune only to remove old or damaged canes at the base, since it spreads gradually by suckers to form a loose colony.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Temple Bells forms a dense, rounded, mid-sized mound smaller than many older Pieris japonica selections.

directions: Grow in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic soil in partial shade sheltered from harsh afternoon sun and winter wind, mulching to hold moisture and soil acidity. Temple Bells produces abundant, long, pendant clusters of pure white, bell-shaped flowers in early spring above glossy dark green foliage, with a fuller flower display than many compact Pieris selections while still staying to a manageable mid-sized mound. Its dense, rounded habit needs little pruning beyond removing spent flower clusters, and it makes a reliable foundation or mixed shrub-border specimen in acid-soil shade gardens.

common_name: Purity Pieris (Large Pure White Flowered Andromeda)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Purity is valued for unusually large, pure white flower clusters on a compact, tidy plant.

directions: Grow in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic soil in partial shade sheltered from harsh afternoon sun and winter wind, mulching to hold moisture and soil acidity. Purity bears exceptionally large, snow-white, urn-shaped flowers in drooping clusters in early to mid spring — noticeably bigger than the blooms of most other Pieris japonica selections — set against glossy dark evergreen foliage on a compact, well-branched habit. Its clean white flower color and refined size make it a strong choice for a shaded foundation planting or woodland-border specimen where a crisp, uncomplicated bloom is wanted. Prune only lightly after flowering to maintain shape.

common_name: Silver Run Leucothoe (Pink-White Variegated Dog Hobble)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade; Silver Run is a variegated sport of native dog hobble with pink, white, and green mottled foliage.

directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade, sheltered from harsh afternoon sun and drying wind, which can scorch the variegated leaves. Silver Run is a striking sport of native drooping leucothoe with arching evergreen foliage marbled in green, pink, and creamy white, brightest on new growth in spring and again in cool fall weather, and deep red-tinged new stems that echo the leaf coloring. Small, white, urn-shaped flowers dangle beneath the arching branches in early spring. It spreads slowly by rhizomes into a graceful, cascading mound, pairing well with ferns and hostas at a woodland border edge, and benefits from occasional removal of old canes at the base to keep new growth vigorous and colorful.
sources: New England Wild Flower Society / Native Plant Trust

common_name: Little Flames Leucothoe (Dwarf Leafscape Compact Dog Hobble)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in fall or spring in moist, strongly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Little Flames is a dwarf branch sport of 'Zeblid' (Scarletta), staying well under two feet tall.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, mulching with pine bark or pine needles to help maintain soil acidity. Little Flames is a compact, low-growing, spreading dwarf discovered as a branch mutation of the popular 'Zeblid' (Scarletta) leucothoe, with the same seasonal color sequence packed into a much smaller frame — bright red new growth in spring, glossy green through summer, and deep burgundy-red in winter, along with fragrant, dangling white, urn-shaped spring flowers. Its diminutive scale suits small foundation beds, rock gardens, and container plantings where the larger species would quickly outgrow the space. Needs little pruning beyond removing the occasional wayward stem to keep its naturally tidy, layered form.

planting.note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; space 6-9 inches apart for ground cover use — Vanilla Chip spreads more slowly and stays smaller than most ajuga cultivars.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Vanilla Chip is a compact, dwarf ajuga selection with small, mint-green leaves that carry a permanent, irregular, pale creamy-yellow margin, giving a soft, two-toned effect distinct from the darker bronze- and purple-leaved ajuga cultivars. In mid to late spring it sends up short, upright spikes of rich blue flowers held just above the foliage mat, providing early nectar for bees. It spreads at a noticeably slower, more restrained pace than many ajuga cultivars, making it easier to keep contained near lawn edges or small garden beds, and its diminutive scale suits rock gardens, path edging, and planting between stepping stones.

planting.note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; space 6-9 inches apart for ground cover use — Mahogany fills in within one to two seasons via stolons.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Mahogany is a standard-sized ajuga selected for its especially dense, dark near-black-burgundy foliage, which emerges glossy in spring and deepens to a rich mahogany tone that holds through the growing season better than many bronze-leaved ajuga cultivars. Short, upright spikes of blue-violet flowers appear in mid-spring, offering early forage for bees above the dark foliage mat. The vigorous, mat-forming, stoloniferous habit fills in quickly and helps suppress weeds and stabilize soil on shaded slopes, though it should be kept away from lawn edges where it can spread into turf. Divide congested patches every few years to maintain vigor and rich leaf color.
